Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says

The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startup DeepSeek , as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.

A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.

The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.

Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.

Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.

DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.

One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.

The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.

The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.

Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the US agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

stories.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
stories.summary: All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket.

About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest.

The rocket’s flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota . The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin .

The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before.

Once around the Earth

The incident was largely forgotten until the last few days, when a farmer in rural Minnesota discovered something unusual while combining his cornfield for the fall harvest. A circular metal object about 11 feet in diameter lay amid the forest of corn stalks in Scott Township, a community in west-central Minnesota.

The Stevens County Sheriff’s Office said it received a phone call reporting the discovery Wednesday.

“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” the Sheriff’s Office wrote on Facebook. “The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field.”

Law enforcement officials said the debris posed no danger to the public. That might not have been true had the object reentered over a more populated area. Space junk routinely falls out of orbit, and fragments of old rockets or satellites sometimes survive the heat of reentry to reach the ground. No one has ever been seriously injured by falling space junk, but there are a few examples of property damage .

Under international law, the country that launched an object into space is liable for any damage it causes on the ground.

What makes the debris in Minnesota unusual is its size —it’s larger than most objects that survive reentry —and the fact that it likely originated from a rocket that fell from space the same day it launched. The upper stage of the Zhuque-2E rocket has a diameter of 11 feet, or 3.35 meters, perfectly matching the size of the object found in Minnesota.

The Zhuque-2E rocket that launched from China on September 15 deployed 10 satellites for the Qianfan, or Thousand Sails, communications network, a Chinese counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. China has launched 258 Qianfan satellites over a series of missions since 2024, on the way to completing an initial constellation of 1,296 satellites, with longer-term ambitions of more than 15,000.

The methane-fueled rocket released the 10 Qianfan satellites into a circular polar orbit at an altitude of roughly 560 miles (900 kilometers) around a half-hour after liftoff. The rocket flew south from China, over Antarctica, then north over the Americas. After deploying its payloads, Zhuque’s upper stage performed a burn to slow its velocity and drop out of orbit.

Normally, deorbiting a spent rocket stage after the end of its mission is a good thing, a responsible practice aimed at limiting the creation of new space debris. Chinese rockets have been a problem in this area before, with unguided reentries and in-orbit breakups in low-Earth orbit. US rockets on low-Earth orbit missions usually reserve enough propellant for guided disposal.

The upper stage from the Zhuque-2E rocket’s previous flight in June broke apart after completing its mission, leaving dozens of pieces of debris in a heavily trafficked part of low-Earth orbit that’s home to the International Space Station and a significant portion of SpaceX’s Starlink broadband network. The good news is the rocket’s altitude was low enough to ensure most of the debris would reenter the atmosphere within a few months.

LandSpace, the company that owns the Zhuque rocket family, has not publicly acknowledged the debris fall over Minnesota. The usual practice for rocket disposals is to steer them toward reentry over the ocean, suggesting the incident on September 15 was perhaps the result of a botched deorbit burn.

stories.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
stories.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 minutes ago

US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts Published 31 August

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.

The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

Google Cloud outage: A summary

Time to recap…

A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London has caused serious failures to services today, affecting operations for several UK banks.

Problems were first detected just after 7am this morning, disrupting “multiple services” in Google’s europe-west2 region (London).

Google blamed the problem on a ‘power issue’ – just afternoon today it said this event had been mitigated. By 1pm UK time services were recovering, and at 3pm Google said services were back online for most customers, with only “a very small number” still affected.

But by that time, millions of customers had been left unable to access and send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC and Revolut .

Revolut said:

double quotation mark “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

A spokesperson for Lloyds added:

double quotation mark “Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Legal proceedings were disrupted, because the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales which failed to work throughout the morning.

The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority , confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage.

This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and Bank of England , since the City watchdogs were handed powers to regulate Google and other rival services that have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.

Tech experts said the outage was another reminder of the dangers of relying on a small number of technology providers for cloud services, a year after problems at Amazon Cloud caused more widespread disruption.

Reynolds: Chinese EV decision will depend on UK interests

Business secretary Johnny Reynolds has insisted any decision to impose tariffs on Chinese EVs will be about British, not EU interests .

He told the business select committee that some were under the misapprehension that the EU wanted the UK to put tariffs on EVs because they feared the Chinese could use Britain as a “backdoor” to the bloc, circumventing trade defence measures including tariffs on EVs and quota on electric hybrid cars.

He point out that this Chinese cars exported from the UK “would not qualify” for duty free exports to the EU under the rules of origin clauses in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement”.

He was also asked about last week’s Franco-German paper proposing that the UK would be included in the upcoming Made in Europe legislation on condition London aligned with EU trade defence measures.

But he said the “detail” of that proposal, which has yet to be adopted by the EU in any new drafting of the Industrial Accelerator Act, “has not been surfaced to the degree to which we’d be able to definitively say that that is what the ask is of the UK.”

Google: We'll publish an analysis of what went wrong

Google add that it does not plan to provide further updates about the outage on its Service Health page – another sign that it thinks it has pretty much resolved the problem with its cloud services today.

It adds:

double quotation mark We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.

Google: issue has been mitigated for most customers

Newsflash: Google has declared that it has won, pretty much, its battle against today’s tech outage at its London-based cloud computing systems.

In an updated status message , Google says:

double quotation mark Multiple services were experiencing issues in the europe-west2 region.

The shift to the past tense is significant – until now, the messages said that services “are” experiencing issues.

Google then declares that all but a few customers have now been helped, saying:

double quotation mark The issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it. If you have questions or are impacted, please open a case with the Support Team and we will work with you until this issue is resolved.

Royal Mail has said it was aware of the issues caused to its services by the Google Cloud outage, and added that there was no effect on letter and parcel deliveries.

Not that those deliveries are always good enough!

Businesss secretary Johnny Reynolds has said he has summoned Royal Mail bosses in for talks to discuss changes to improve the services, my colleague Lisa O’Carroll reports.

He told a parliamentary business committee that the Royal Mail is not delivering “the level of service people expect”.

Royal Mail have not met their first or second class standards for almost 10 years, the committee heard.

Reynolds said the government had negotiated the take over by Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year which included a curb on dividends “until performance improved”.

“I know for parliamentarians this in oral questions on Thursday and other correspondence with members of Parliament that it is one of the most significant issues they’re facing,” Reynolds told the committee.

He said the government “recognised the need for regulatory reform” but Ofcom was taking a lead at the moment on this subject.

double quotation mark “I am going to have Royal Mail and the unions in for a conversation about this. I need to respond to what MPs are being told. “Royal Mail is a really important institution and business, and I know it has significant ramifications when it’s not hitting the levels of service. And I can promise you, chair, whether it’s work with Ofcom, whether it’s work with, with, you know, any part, any key player, any stakeholder in this, we will do what we can to make sure Royal Mail is the service it needs to be.”

Lloyds: expect services to get back to normal soon

Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax, is hopeful that services will be restored soon.

A spokesperson for Lloyds tells us:

double quotation mark “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to all our services back to normal soon.”

UK regulators want answers from Google about Cloud outage

The Financial Conduct Authority and Bank of England are pushing Google for details of today’s cloud services outage, as they face their first major test as new regulators of “critical” tech suppliers to UK banks.

Both the FCA and Bank of England were handed powers in July to start directly overseeing the local arms of Google Cloud and three other Silicon Valley rivals - Amazon Web Services, Oracle and Microsoft – after being designated as critical third parties by the UK government, as their services become a crucial part of increasingly digital banking services.

A spokesperson for the FCA said they were in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm about the service outage which began this morning ( details start here ).

The watchdogs are in charge of ensuring that the cloud providers are resilient and actively reducing the risk of cyber-attacks and major outages like the one experienced today, which has disrupted services for millions of people and businesses across the UK.

For its part, Google is meant to prove it is carrying out proper stress testing, including how it would respond to imagined emergency scenarios that would put their operations under severe strain. They’re also meant to have reported any major incidents, including this power outages, to the two regulators (though it’s unclear in what time frame).

Low-paid workers and hospitality firms face disruption

The failure of banking apps due to the Google Cloud outage could disproportionately affect those most struggling with the cost of living, argues audit, tax and business advisory firm Blick Rothenberg .

Blick Rothenberg partner Andrew Sanford explains:

double quotation mark “Weekly or fortnightly paid employees, often those on lower wages, may have found that they are unable to access their funds on the very day where they have payments or commitments to make.” “The hospitality sector will also be disproportionately impacted by those people affected by the outage with no means of making payment, who simply do not go the pub or restaurant.”

Affected companies coming back online again

There are signs that the companies affected by Google’s outage are getting online again.

Emma , the personal finance, budgeting, and money management app which was taken down by the Google Cloud outage ( see 10.11am ), has posted on X that it is operating again.

Emma says:

double quotation mark We’re back ✅ Emma is up and running again after this morning’s Google Cloud power outage in London . Your data and money were safe throughout. Some balances may take a little while to refresh. Thanks for your patience 💜

Google: We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads

Newsflash: Google says service ​are being ‌restored ‌in its London-based ‌cloud region after today’s outage.

The company says:

double quotation mark “We are seeing the recovery of services for most workloads in europe-west2.”

This isn’t the end of the story, though – Google are promising another update by 3pm UK time.

Google added that they will provide an update by 06:00 PDT (2pm BST) with “current details” of the situation.

Google: The power event is mitigated

Newsflash: Google says the ‘power event’ which affected its London-based cloud computing operating and caused widepread disruption to services in the UK has been ‘mitigated’.

In a new statement on its Service Health page, Google reports seeing signs that services are being restored.

It says:

double quotation mark A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads. Full recovery of existing workloads should be completed, tentatively by Tuesday, 2026-10-20 06:00 [Pacific Daylight Time].

[ CORRECTED: 6am PDT is 2pm UK time.]

The Google Cloud outage could result in some companies losing sales, and they might struggle to get much compensation, suggests Ryan Gracey , partner at law firm Gordons.

double quotation mark “Many businesses will be discovering today that their cloud contracts protect the supplier far more than they protect the customer. “When a provider goes down, the usual remedy is a modest credit against future fees. That is small consolation set against lost revenue, frustrated customers and damage to reputation. “Liability for those wider losses is typically capped or excluded altogether. The real exposure sits in the gap between how heavily a business depends on its provider and how little its contract actually guarantees. For banks, the stakes are higher still. Regulators expect them to keep essential services running even when a key supplier fails. “Outsourcing a service does not mean outsourcing responsibility for it. Boards should be asking, not just what their contracts promise, but whether the business could keep going if its provider went dark for a day.”

Google: power event disrupted our Cloud services

Google are blaming a ‘power event’ for the disruption at its London-based Cloud computing operations today.

In an update on its status page, Google says:

double quotation mark Due to a power event we had suffered an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. Partial mitigation to infrastructure services will be observed within the next 30 minutes and the remaining services will be mitigated there after.

PA: Court hearings delayed as nationwide video system goes down

The video system used by courts across England and Wales went down on Tuesday in an issue believed to be linked to the wider Google outage, the Press Association report.

The Cloud Video Platform (CVP), which is used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely, was not functioning throughout the morning.

Users expecting to attend court on video link were met with a message saying there was an internal server error.

The issue is expected to have left many hearings across the country delayed or unable to go ahead as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody to attend court.

The judge in the Russell Brand trial, Mr Justice Bennathan, decided to press on with proceedings at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday morning despite the link being broken.

Some journalists who would have been watching online were squeezed into extra seats in court, but many were not able to follow the proceedings as the fourth complainant started her evidence.

Staff at the court said there was a national outage and did not know when it would be resolved.

It is understood to be linked to an outage affecting Google’s Cloud network, which affected businesses including online bank Revolut , delivery service DPD and Royal Mail.

The nature of cloud ecosystems mean that a problem in one region can ripple out and cause widesread disruption.

Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad , lecturer in computer science at Keele University , explains:

double quotation mark “Another outage, another reminder of the fragility of cloud infrastructure. Google Cloud is currently experiencing a major incident affecting the europe-west2 (London) region, with elevated errors and intermittent network failures impacting more than 38 cloud-native services across key categories including Compute & Containers, Storage & Databases, Analytics & Data Processing, Networking & Connectivity, Messaging & Streaming, Caching & Memory Services, and AI/Platform Services. “Google Engineers are actively investigating the issue and testing mitigations, including moving impacted workloads to alternative regions where feasible. The disruption has also affected several major organisations and financial institutions that rely on the affected region. “More importantly, the incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures. “A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centred on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures.”

A Lloyds spokesperson has confirmed the bank (which includes Halifax) has experienced problems today:

double quotation mark “Our app is online and customers can log in normally, though we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning. We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely.”

Google’s latest update on its Cloud outage reiterates what we knew already.

It says:

double quotation mark We apologize to all who are affected by the disruption. Symptoms Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region. Note: Looker Studio is not impacted by this outage. Workaround If feasible, the impacted customer may try to migrate their workload impacted to another available location (zone or region).

stories.title: Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader
stories.summary: Dodds said it was time to hand over the leadership to a "new generation" after nearly nine years in the role.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Jane Dodds has been a Senedd member since 2021 and became Welsh Lib Dem leader in 2017

Published 20 October 2026, 18:21 BST

Jane Dodds has announced she will stand down as leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats.

Dodds said she would remain the party's only Member of the Senedd (MS), but that work to increase its presence in Wales' parliament "should be led by a new generation".

"Leading the Welsh Liberal Democrats has been the honour of my life," she said in a statement on Tuesday, adding "now is the right time" to hand over the role.

Only Welsh Lib Dem MP David Chadwick is eligible to seek nomination to replace Dodds at this stage, the party said.

Relations between Dodds and the UK Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey were strained after he previously called her leadership into question.

The Liberal Democrats have been represented by just one member in Cardiff Bay since 2016, initially by former Welsh Lib Dem leader Kirsty Williams and later by Dodds since 2021.

Dodds, who represents Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd in the Senedd, is a former social worker who was made her party's Welsh leader in November 2017.

She made headlines last year by getting the previous Welsh Labour government to agree to a greyhound racing ban and £1 bus fares for under-21s in return for helping it pass its budget.

In 2024 Lib Dem leader Sir Ed asked Dodds to reflect on her position over her handling of a sexual abuse case when she worked for the Church in England.

A 2021 report found Dodds made a "grave error of judgement" by not organising a meeting to discuss a particular case of abuse by a late former bishop who sexually abused at least 18 victims over a 15-year period.

Dodds accepted there were "shortcomings", but said she would continue as leader.

After nearly two years of cool relations over the matter, Davey backed Dodds before May's Welsh Parliament election, describing her as an "excellent member of the Senedd" who deserved to be re-elected.

Nominations to replace Dodds will open on 23 October and close on 16 November.

"After May's election, I've thought hard about what our party needs," she said.

"Wales needs more than one liberal voice in the Senedd.

"Building that team will take years of hard work in communities across the country, and I believe that work should be led by a new generation.

"Now is the right time to hand it over."

Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe MP Chadwick said Dodds had "given an enormous amount to the Welsh Liberal Democrats and to public life in Wales, and she deserves our sincere thanks for her service as leader".

"There will understandably be questions about what comes next.

"Today should be about Jane and her contribution to our party.

"I will make a statement about my own political future in the coming days."

Welsh Liberal Democrat president Tim Sly said Dodds had "led our party with warmth, determination and integrity through some of the most turbulent years in Welsh and UK politics".

"She leaves the Welsh Liberal Democrats stronger in our communities and ready to build," he said.

Chadwick requires the support of 50 party members to be the only candidate to replace Dodds and take over as leader.

Should that not happen, or he were to decide not to run, all members on the party's approved parliamentary candidates list could then throw their hats into the ring.

These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?

W ho knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.

For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.

Downstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).

Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.

No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?

Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.

The trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The 2026 GOB counts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.

Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).

And so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …

Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and the tricolore of Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. He made the news in June when hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.

To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”

Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”

I n a 2024 study , Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.

Oxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.

Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones use more than 500 litres of diesel per hour , releasing CO 2 as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about 16m tonnes of CO 2 annually . It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO 2 . In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.

And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.

Ecocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”

Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”

Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capitalist class” who operate outside and above borders and rules. Look at the stern of the superyachts, under the name, and they’re almost all registered in places such as the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, the Isle of Man and Malta – flag states offering, among other benefits, tax neutrality.

It’s hard to hide a superyacht, or ownership of one. We know about Mark Zuckerberg’s 118-metre Launchpad, and Jeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru, estimated to have cost €444m. Koru caused a stir in 2022, when a historic bridge in Rotterdam, a Dutch national monument, was going to be dismantled in order to let it through. After the uproar its masts were stepped downstream in the end. Koru is actually a sailing yacht, which might sound like a greener way of doing it, but then Bezos also has a 75-metre support vessel, with additional crew accommodation, helipad, submarine, speedboats and cars, that follows Koru around like a loyal dog. Zuckerberg’s got a couple of support vessels too.

Roman Abramovich is another big fan of a yacht. Using leaked documents, Forbes counted 16 belonging to the Russian oligarch. My ship location app tells me that the superest of his fleet – Solaris (140-metres) and Eclipse (162-metres), both registered in the Cook Islands – are now parked in the Sea of Marmara, near Istanbul. When western governments seized Russian oligarchs’ assets after the invasion of Ukraine, Turkey refused to join the sanctions and became a bolt-hole.

Eclipse doesn’t even eclipse everything. The world’s longest superyacht, at 180-metres, is Azzam, launched in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, who died in 2022, but according to Boat International and the Superyacht Fan website , Azzam is still in the family. When you get to this level it’s not always clear who owns a yacht, as they can be held in trusts or shell companies, sometimes across several jurisdictions.

Take Dilbar for example – a little shorter than Azzam but the world’s largest by volume. In June Bloomberg reported that a court in Germany had ruled that sanctions no longer applied to the yacht after finding insufficient evidence that the Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov controls The Sister Trust, which formally owns the vessel.

Or Kosatka, formerly Graceful, the 82-metre yacht seen being escorted through Danish waters by Russian naval vessels in the summer and widely reported to be linked to Vladimir Putin. A bigger, 140-metre yacht, the €620m Scheherazade, which boasts two helipads, anti-drone technology and a cryotherapy room, remains impounded in Italy. Activists working for poisoned Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny believe that one is also owned by Putin.

T here is no secret about who owns the aptly named Leviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show. Co-founder and president of the video game company Valve, Gabe Newell doesn’t just own the 111-metre Leviathan, he also owns the 93-metre support vessel Draak, parked up next door.

I am allowed on to Leviathan and get a brief look around. I’m shown the huge mess area, which Newell and his guests share with the 42 crew. As well as the pool, there’s an outdoor cinema, basketball court, and a huge gaming lounge with consoles and race simulators, open to everyone. The crew are also keen to point out Leviathan’s diesel-electric hybrid propulsion and battery energy storage system. But it still has a 494,000-litre fuel tank. Fill ’er up? Certainly sir, that’ll be roughly a million euros.

It’s not total eco denial at the Monaco Yacht Show however, there’s at least some acknowledgment of environmental impact. I drop in on the Blue Wake awards, “for solutions delivering measurable impact on yachting sustainability”. So there’s a prize for a company using more sustainable materials for yacht interiors. A yacht wins a Blue Wake for having sails, and a marina gets one for planting Posidonia plants.

This is all good news … but actually, when you look at it, it’s not that good. In five years 3,000 sq metres of Posidonia have been restored – sounds impressive, but then by my calculations that’s an area of about 55 metres by 55 metres. The boat with sails? Great, but actually there are fewer sailing boats here than in previous years, the trend is towards power, more and more of it.

It looks like greenwashing, token gestures. I have an Italian friend who calls these superyachts stronzi di mare – turds of the sea. And you know what you can’t do to a turd. There’s no escaping the truth: that they drink fossil fuels like there’s no tomorrow, which there won’t be if they’re allowed to carry on; that there’s no more monstrous symbol of inequality; and that they look like irons.

But before storming off in disgust, maybe I’ll just pop into that wine tasting. In my socks.

stories.body:
Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong

D oes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.

Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal . European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.

The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House . Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , are no substitute for answers.

A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “ strategically and culturally vital ”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881 , the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage spoke at a rally in Plymouth

Published 2 hours ago

The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, has told a rally in Plymouth he would get rid of tax on pay for armed forces reservists.

Farage said he wanted to get more people in the reserves at the event for party supporters as part of Reform's 100 Days to Save Britain tour.

When questioned by the BBC over a Reform councillor in Plymouth who was investigated and cleared over social media posts, Farage said he was "still part of the party was because everyone believes he's a solid bloke".

About 100 protesters against Reform gathered outside the Plymouth Arena near the city centre, chanting before, during and after the event.

Reform leader Nigel Farage greeting supporters at the rally in Plymouth

Farage spoke to about 300 Reform members and councillors and opened his speech by paying tribute to Ann Widdecombe, who was killed at her home in Devon .

On cutting tax for reservists, he said: "Anyone that signs up as a reservist and does their bit will face no tax on the pay they receive.

"Let's get more men and women signing up for the reserves."

When asked by the BBC about the UK deploying fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia , Farage said the UK was "not even a player any more".

He said: "Should we help with peacekeeping missions? As much as we can.

"But what we've got to face up to is the reality that we've lost our ability to be an effective player".

More news stories for Devon

Listen to the latest news for Devon

Plymouth Reform councillor Ben Rowe was investigated in May after being accused of sharing Islamophobic posts on social media but was then cleared.

The BBC asked Farage if Rowe's behaviour had been acceptable.

He said: "These are working class people, going into politics, venting their spleen on certain issues and maybe there's a little bit of political growing up to do.

"But let's not condemn everybody for everything they say, and the reason he's still part of the party is because everyone believes he's a solid bloke."

Pretesters against the rally gathered outside Plymouth Arena

Outside the event, amid a significant police presence, protesters gathered with placards and joined in chants saying Farage was not welcome in the city.

Liam Condron-Farnos, from the campaign group Stand Up To Racism, said: "The way he's built his politics over the years, and still is, is on anti-immigrant hysteria.

"We need to show him that's not an uncontested view in this country."

stories.title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
stories.summary: This post was co-written by Andi Cao , an EFF legal intern. Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives. Cities should not buy them , and cities that already have them should shut them down. Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights. A warrant requires a judge to find probable cause and specificity—many warrantless police searches of ALPR data lack both. Officers have searched this data to profile Romani people, monitor protesters, investigate an abortion, find immigrants for deportation, track a man who complained about a deputy, stalk romantic partners, and even for no stated reason beyond “LMAO.” A warrant requirement would force law enforcement to justify these searches before accessing sensitive location records, not leave the people they target to discover and challenge the abuse after the harm is done. What a Warrant Requires Warrants are a check on police power. Before officers can search a person or their property, the Fourth Amendment requires them to convince a neutral judge, under oath, that probable cause exists, meaning a fair probability the search will turn up evidence of a crime. The warrant must also describe with particularity what will be searched, so police cannot go on a fishing expedition. Critically, the officer who wants to search is not the person who decides whether the search is justified. That is why warrants are required for so many kinds of police surveillance. For example, police generally need a warrant to wiretap phone calls , to search the contents of a cell phone , and to obtain historical cell phone location records . Whether you want to protect yourself from data brokers or just don’t want Big Tech profiting off your browsing data, Privacy Badger is here to help. Install Privacy Badger Support the Fight Against Online Tracking Safari support has been one of Privacy Badger’s most requested features for years. stories.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
stories.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. stories.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
stories.summary: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 October 2026, 06:00 BST

President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.

Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.

The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.

So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.

1. US economy growing

The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.

The latest data shows US GDP , external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.

And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.

That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.

The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) , external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.

It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.

Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.

The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.

Spending on building data centres , external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.

2. Inflation picked up

Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.

The current rate of US inflation , external is 3.7%.

That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.

Economists estimate , external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.

While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.

The price of a gallon of diesel in the US , external - a fuel used not only by drivers but also widely in agriculture and industry - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.

The price of some grocery staples , external like beef and coffee have risen since Trump returned to office, though the price of eggs has fallen.

And some US retailers have warned , external that rising energy prices caused by the Iran war will make producing food more expensive and raise prices at the till.

3. Household income growth held back

Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.

The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record , external .

However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following , external on US households:

- Trump's tax cuts

- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans

- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war

ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.

The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.

ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank , external .

4. Job creation slowed down

Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs" , external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.

Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.

​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency , external .

And the number of Americans employed in manufacturing , external - 12.6 million in September 2026 - is slightly lower than it was when Trump's second term began.

However, the US unemployment rate remains relatively low , external at 4.2%, which is broadly where it was when Trump returned to the White House.

Part of the reason for this is Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation programme, which has reduced the size of the available US workforce , external and means a lower number of jobs need to be created each month to stop unemployment rising.

5. Borrowing costs rising

US government borrowing has increased in Trump's second term, partly driven up by his significant tax cuts .

The federal government deficit - the gap between its revenues from taxes and its spending - was $2 trillion in the year to September 2026 , external . That's equivalent to around 6% , external of US GDP.

And the US deficit is projected to rise to above 8% of GDP by 2030 , external .

That high rate of government borrowing is itself helping to boost US GDP growth.

The IMF has warned that excessive US government borrowing , external , which it uses to bridge the deficit, and its rapidly rising national debt are raising the risk of a future financial crisis in America. This would have a deeply damaging impact on most American households.

The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.

The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.

That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.

The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4% , external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.

That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates , external and cannot take with them to a new property.

ITV’s newly released documentary Undercover: A Year in Reform has raised fresh questions about Nigel Farage’s party, after covertly recorded footage showed councillors and candidates making racist, Islamophobic, misogynistic and violent remarks. The investigation also exposed the party’s vetting procedures and internal discussions about controversial candidates.

The immediate consequences have included resignations and suspensions of Reform UK councillors and candidates. But whether the documentary’s revelations will translate into lost votes is less certain.

The documentary’s significance lies partly in the questions it raises about organisational responsibility. Reform has said it has improved its vetting procedures since the 2024 general election and insists that there is “no room for racism” in its ranks. Farage, meanwhile, has argued that parties cannot vet people for everything they might say in the future.

The disciplinary position is not uniform. According to ITV’s published account of what has happened to those councillors and candidates featured in the documentary, several have since resigned from their posts or the party, while others remain in place.

Aspiring parliamentary candidate Jason Powell was suspended by Reform after recordings emerged of him advocating the building of concentration camps to house migrants who arrive on small boats. He also said that Muslims cannot be British.

The revelations raise a broader question. Do voters regard the remarks of Reform councillors and candidates as as isolated acts of misconduct, or evidence of a problem with the party itself?

The gap between perceptions and votes

Polling from before the documentary’s release offers a useful starting point. In October 2025, YouGov found that 47% of Britons considered Reform UK generally racist, while 43% said the same of its voters. The same YouGov poll found that 90% of Reform voters considered the party generally not racist, 88% said the same of its policies and 87% considered Reform voters to be generally not racist.

These findings reveal a divide between Reform supporters and the wider electorate. But they don’t establish whether the party’s supporters approve of racist remarks. YouGov research found that 86% of Reform supporters considered immigration a major national issue, while 35–39% cited perceived honesty or the need for political change to be among the party’s attractions. However, polling cannot establish whether these voters would overlook racist remarks in making their voting decisions.

The latest widely reported YouGov poll on voting intention figures, conducted on October 11–12, put Reform at 21%. With the documentary initially being broadcast on October 18, the figures taken before the broadcast provide a baseline for future voting intentions. But it’s not yet clear whether the ITV documentary will now have discouraged people from voting Reform.

What happened when Ukip faced similar scrutiny?

The UK Independent Party’s (Ukip) experience in 2014-15 provides a useful, if imperfect, historical comparison, due to a similar series of controversies involving candidates’ remarks.

William Henwood, a council candidate, tweeted that comedian Lenny Henry should emigrate to “a black country”, prompting his resignation from the party. Andre Lampitt, who appeared in Ukip’s European election broadcast, was suspended after racist and islamaphobic tweets emerged.

Other candidates came under scrutiny for comments about Islam and the murder of Stephen Lawrence, while The Guardian newspaper revealed that one candidate’s Facebook page showed a “like” for a group devoted to the far-right British National Party.

On May 7 2014, Farage rejected accusations that Ukip was racist , arguing that the controversial remarks of a small number of candidates did not represent the party as a whole.

An ITV News/ComRes poll surveying 2,052 British adults the previous month reported that 32% of respondents considered Ukip to be a racist party. Yet among people who said they were likely to vote in the European elections in May, Ukip received the most support with 38% – although its share fell to 32% when a broader group of likely voters was included.

A separate YouGov poll published days later put Ukip on 29% for the European elections.

Together, these polls suggested that concerns about racism can coexist with strong electoral support, but couldn’t establish whether the controversies reduced Ukip’s support. When votes were counted on May 22, the party won 27.5% of the vote in Great Britain and 24 seats in the European parliament.

The polls differed in their timing and methods, and were unable to isolate the effect of the allegations. Nevertheless, they demonstrated that substantial reputational concerns could coexist with strong electoral support. Ukip’s opponents could persuade many people that the party attracted racist candidates – but this didn’t necessarily affect the amount of votes they received. Nor can we tell how Ukip might have performed without the controversies.

The electoral test yet to come

For Reform, any political consequences of revelations about their representatives can’t be inferred from public condemnation alone.

The crucial distinction is between disapproval and defection. Research suggests that voters’ responses to political controversies depend partly on their existing party loyalties and their tolerance of political misconduct. A 2014 study based on British survey data, found that both factors shaped how people judged political controversies.

More recently, a 2026 study found that well-substantiated evidence of misconduct during the Partygate scandal was associated with less favourable evaluations of the governing Conservative Party and reduced voting intentions . Even loyal voters may punish a party when evidence of misconduct is clear.

Neither voter loyalty nor the severity of a controversy alone determine its electoral consequences. Some voters may discount allegations against a party they support, while others may reconsider when evidence is clear and responsibility is apparent. Whether voters prioritise a party’s policies over the conduct of its candidates also cannot be assumed.

Establishing the documentary’s effects on perceptions of Reform’s credibility, or their organisational competence, would require polling that directly measures public reactions as well as subsequent voting intentions. It is too early to conclude that the programme has either damaged Reform electorally, or left its support unchanged.

The central question is not simply whether voters condemn racism, but whether they regard the controversy as important enough to change their political choices. Ukip’s experience shows why that relationship cannot be assumed. For Reform, the longer-term test will be whether voters continue to see these incidents as individual failings, or increasingly associate them with the party’s organisation and leadership.

Nigel Farage

And so France continues to smoulder. Two weeks after the first mass demonstrations in support of increased funding for French state schools, events reached a peak on Saturday October 17. Widespread destruction of small businesses, cafés, town halls and chain shops have brought the French economy even further to catastrophe.

The scenes of mass looting, along with the burning spire of the 150-year-old Limoges town hall hardly inspire confidence in the government of President Emmanuel Macron and his prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu. A sell-off of government bonds is the latest sign of economic gloom, demonstrating the market’s concerns over France’s ability to claw back control over its public finances.

It is easy to forget there is a legitimate reason for these protests: educational reform. This was also the root cause for the events of May and June 1968, which this generation of protesters have looked to emulate. Although changes to the education system were introduced in the wake of May 1968, the centre-right went onto win a majority in the June parliamentary elections in a wave of support for General Charles de Gaulle, rather than in support of the protesters’ cause.

Macron now faces similar problems to de Gaulle, with the cost of living and youth unemployment also part of the picture. When he came to power in May 2017, Macron promised major investment in education and skills . But a report by the French Cour des Comptes , an independent court which monitors public spending, concluded that this investment has had no major impact on improving access to work.

The demonstrators are rightly concerned about the cost of living and the absence of meaningful investment in schools on the margins of major cities. The irony, of course, is that the destruction of businesses in the latest, violent, demonstrations, will probably push the cost of living up, not down.

The impact on tourism, for example, will be considerable, given that some other countries, while stopping short of an outright travel ban, have warned people to exercise caution when travelling to France.

Economy in peril

In 2018, in the wake of the gilets jaunes protests , Macron reversed his previous position of balancing tax cuts with spending cuts and introduced €10 billion (£8.85 billion) worth of measures designed to mitigate the cost of living, including raising the minimum wage and removing tax on overtime payments.

Macron’s disastrous decision to call the summer 2024 parliamentary elections has caused political stalemate in the National Assembly. And, with debt of at least 115% of GDP and a deficit of 5.1% of GDP, the French economy is already deeply burdened. So Macron can ill afford to spend his way out of trouble. To make matters worse, more than 50% of French debt is held by foreign investors – and a bond sell-off is already underway following the weekend’s protests.

What, then, can Macron and Lecornu actually achieve? There is little way out of this financial black hole without tax rises and major cuts to welfare. Clearly a tougher conversation on the French public finances, especially in terms of the very generous retirement packages enjoyed by many over-60s in France, is required.

What this means for the 2027 election

All the while Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the candidates of extreme-right and extreme-left, are already campaigning ahead of the presidential election in April 2027. Macron is essentially a lame duck. He cannot stand for a further term and, in any case, would have little to no chance of winning.

But this episode won’t have helped his fragile centrist coalition. And the recent imposition of a curfew by Lecornu and the unpopular interior minister Laurent Nuñez is unlikely to endear the government to voters concerned by recent violence.

Le Pen’s party, Rassemblement National (RN), has long campaigned on the theme of law and order and she has sought to use the riots to cement her position as the only leader capable of restoring peace to the streets. Le Pen released a video message in which she sat in front of the French national flag, le drapeau tricolore , and promised that the people of France would have their chance to vote for a new era of “restored authority and security”.

By contrast, Mélenchon and his party, La France Insoumise (LFI or France Unbowed) have identified with the protests since they began. The risk is that, while being seen to sympathise with the very real concerns of the protest movement, the LFI and its leader risk being implicated in the violence playing out on news bulletins across the country and globally. Whether this will convince floating voters to back him at the 2027 presidential elections remains unclear.

The choice now appears to be between two extremes rather than the centre ground, given the collapse of the centre-right Republican party and the centre-left Socialist party following Macron’s 2017 victory.

The leading centrist candidates, Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, both former prime ministers under Macron, have plummeted in the polls in recent days and their Ensemble coalition, at 15% Of the vote is a distant third compared with Mélenchon’s leftwing Nouveau Front populaire , on 24%, and Le Pen’s RN, on 34%.

For both centrist candidates the protests are likely to serve as a reminder to maintain distance from the dying Macron administration. They will also be hoping that the economic picture improves before next May, when the French people go to the polls.
