stories.title: PM says youth unemployment is a 'catastrophe and a moral failure'
stories.summary: The UK faces "economic catastrophe" with one million young people not in work or training, the prime minister says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Britain needs to "invest in the success of our young people", Andy Burnham says

Published 19 October 2026

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Writing in the Times newspaper , external , Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.

This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.

Around 39% are unemployed while the remaining 61% are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.

The number of 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits stands at 331,000, almost double the number in 2016, but lower than the peaks of around 500,000 seen after the financial crisis in 2008 and Covid in 2020.

The UK government will spend £353bn on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is spent on benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments.

In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.

Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.

"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."

He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".

"We either invest in the success of our young people or pay for failure through the benefits system. We cannot afford to do both," Burnham wrote.

Ministers are this week set to release plans for 22,400 apprenticeships a year in businesses such as accountants, legal services and consultants, in addition to 40,000 placements in the construction industry.

The Conservative shadow business and trade secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."

The party has said they would cut £36bn a year from the welfare budget including by reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit and restricting who receives housing benefit.

Green Party deputy co-leader Mothin Ali accused Labour of planning a "welfare cuts charter that would take support away from young people who are already struggling and vulnerable".

What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many? Published 27 August

Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor Published 28 September

Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".

While the prime minister has emphasised the importance of incentivising young people into work, the review's author Alan Milburn suggested there could be cuts to benefits.

The former health secretary told the Guardian , external that there was a need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support".

"This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."

Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful" .

In order to cut the benefit bill, both Burnham and Milburn will need to secure the support of those Labour MPs who previously baulked at Sir Keir Starmer's attempts to reduce spending by £5bn a year.

Backbenchers objected to proposals to tighten restrictions for those claiming working-age health-related benefits and, following a rebellion, the then-prime minister was forced to abandon his plans.

Two of Burnham's closest supporters Louise Haigh, his effective deputy, and Anneliese Midgley, his chief whip, who are now in government, were both leading lights in the welfare rebellion.

But difficult decisions are coming nonetheless and government insiders are clear that the link between cuts to welfare entitlement to fund increased jobs support is inevitable.

While Burnham has promised not to introduce "crude cuts", Labour advisers say it is impossible to leave the system for under 25s unchanged.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden is sympathetic to Milburn's call for a new, parallel benefits system for young people - but that level of change will require legislation.

Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, and there is not expected to be much mention of welfare in it.

Instead a bill is being prepared and the New Year is when that is likely to be voted on by MPs.

stories.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
stories.summary: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026

Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

There have been laws against playing loud music, as well as singing, on trains since 2005 but the government will remind rail passengers of this with the launch of a national campaign asking people to "share the carriage, not the noise".

The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

The rail campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000.

The government also said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crack down on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the transport secretary.

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff "or the British Transport Police if they wish".

"They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said.

Justin from Newcastle-upon-Tyne, welcomed the proposal but wanted to know how it would be enforced.

He told the BBC noise on public transport had stopped him from using buses "due to the levels of antisocial behaviour including this unwanted attendance to someone's social media doom scrolling audio concert".

He said he'd "much rather enjoy my own company with my own music in the isolation of my car".

Transport for London, which operates London Underground, already has by-laws in place to prohibit people playing music or content aloud.

It said that in the first instance enforcement officers will ask the passenger to stop.

"Most people comply at this stage," it said, but added that if someone refuses, they may be asked to leave the train or they could be reported for possible prosecution.

The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".

However, she added the government must "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers".

"Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.

Dave McAra from Derby got in touch with the BBC to raise a similar point: "Who is going to police this legislation on a bus? The solo driver? I think not as he would probably be verbally abused at best and assaulted at worst."

Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise Published 6 August

Reported assaults on Britain's rail services rise by more than a third Published 24 September

Safety concerns put Londoners off buses, say Tories Published 11 July

Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with different accessibility needs.

He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."

Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the Conservative Party had "led the charge" against antisocial behaviour on public transport last year.

However, he added passengers and railway staff faced more serious problems.

"Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways," he said.

Liberal Democrat transport spokesperson Olly Glover said: "Unless the government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."

Independent watchdog Transport Focus said its research showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway.

"Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell from Transport Focus.

"Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

stories.body:
Latest ONS data presents mixed picture amid slump in job vacancies and analysts warning labour market is ‘running on idle’

Business live – news updates

Healey to reject calls to raise CGT in budget

Unemployment in the UK has fallen unexpectedly in the final snapshot of the jobs market before John Healey’s first budget next week.

The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics . City economists had forecast a rise to 5%.

In a further boost to the chancellor, the figures also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3 million.

However, a slump in the number of job vacancies illustrated what some economists said was an economy moving sideways. After hitting a peak of 1.3m in the period after the pandemic, vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic.

Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation thinktank at Lancaster University, said the fall in unemployment “should not make the government complacent ahead of next week’s budget”.

He said: “The UK is still amid a jobs drought with vacancies at their lowest for over 12 years outside of the pandemic.”

Vacancies fell particularly sharply across the construction sector, suggesting Britain’s builders cut back on hiring last summer.

Data on wage growth was mixed. Stripping out bonuses, average pay growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6%. However, when bonuses are included the rate fell to 3.7% from 3.9%, indicating that only a few workers received bonuses.

Wage growth in the UK remains above inflation, which was 3.1% in August and is expected to rise to 3.4% when figures for September are published on Wednesday. The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates in response to higher prices at next month’s meeting of the monetary policy committee (MPC).

The pound rose against the dollar after the labour market figures were released, by about half a cent to $1.3352, as investors bet on the increased likelihood of a rate rise from 3.75% as early as next month.

Members of the MPC are split on the need for further increases in the cost of borrowing with some, including the Columbia University professor Alan Taylor, arguing that the committee needs to wait several months to see whether costs and wages continue to rise.

Financial markets expect interest rates to rise to between 4.75% and 5% by the middle of next year, although the consultancy Capital Economics said recent improvements in the labour market were modest and the central bank would probably cap interest rates at 4.25%.

Ellie Henderson, an economist at Investec, said lower unemployment and higher wages would make a majority of the MPC nervous about leaving interest rates on hold.

“The MPC will collectively decide to increase the Bank rate by 0.25 percentage points at the next meeting in November, framing it as a ‘risk management’ move, in case the data were to turn or energy prices move even higher,” she said.

“Sterling markets seem to agree, with the pound strengthening on the numbers, gaining modestly against both the US dollar and the euro.”

Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, described the labour market as “running on idle” with employers limiting recruitment and pay awards “in response to surging cost pressures and pre-budget policy uncertainty”.

He said: “The continued fall in vacancies is a flashing red warning light for the labour market, suggesting that a damaging side-effect of this year’s AI-fuelled economic growth has been weaker hiring demand, compounded by elevated employment costs.”

The ONS estimated there were 715,000 unemployed young people aged 16 to 24, down by 28,000 on the quarter.

Harrison of the Work Foundation welcomed the drop, but said ministers should be more focused on the number of jobless young people remaining at 54,000 higher than 12 months ago.

The secretary of state for work and pensions, Pat McFadden, said: “Today’s figures show the resilience of our labour market with unemployment falling and the UK’s employment rate now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty.”

But he conceded that many young people needed support to enter the labour market. “That’s why we are working with industry, to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system.”

stories.body:
Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys

T here are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment for Donald Trump is poor but small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood.

Confidence is generally stable.

This week, the National Federation of Independent Businesses said that its Small Business Optimism Index fell to just below its long-term average, while uncertainty rose slightly. Labor quality was the top concern for 26% of owners and inflation for 20%. Expansion plans weakened, though 17% still plan to add jobs during the next three months.

However, small-business confidence improved significantly in the third quarter, according to the recently published Justworks/US Chamber Small Business Index . Some 72% of the 750 small businesses surveyed say they are comfortable with their current cash flow, but only 27% believe the US economy is in good health. Inflation remains the biggest problem, cited by 54% of owners.

Hiring is not strong, but not weak either.

HR platform Gusto estimated that small businesses added 28,000 jobs in September, making it the eighth consecutive month of employment gains following a decline in January. According to the company’s data, hiring accelerated from August’s revised gain of 18,500 jobs and growth was broad across industries, regions and company sizes, with healthcare and social assistance among the strongest sectors. Particularly notable is that some of the smallest employers continue to participate in the expansion, rather than job growth being concentrated solely among larger companies.

In its latest Small Business Employment Watch report, Paychex, another large HR and payroll processing service (and a client of my company), said that hiring in September essentially matched its 2026 year-to-date average with overall employment among companies with fewer than 50 employees appearing “stable”.

ADP , the country’s largest HR and payroll processing service, reported that US private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, with hiring accelerating for the first time since May following three months of slowing growth. Education and healthcare and leisure and hospitality led the gains, while financial activities and professional and business services were weaker. Importantly for small businesses, establishments employing one to 19 workers added 18,000 jobs. According to ADP, private-sector employers have not shifted into recession mode and although hiring has cooled from earlier periods, businesses are still adding employees.

Intuit painted a slightly different jobs picture. Its Intuit QuickBooks Small Business Index , which is based on data it gathers from its millions of QuickBooks customers, found that employment at US businesses with one to nine employees fell by 7,000 jobs in September and that jobs declined across most sectors and regions.

Revenues remain solid.

Intuit’s QuickBooks data shows that revenues moved sharply up this past month as inflation-adjusted average monthly revenue increased 1.68% and growth occurring in 11 of 12 industries, every region and 19 of 20 states.

Fiserv , a payment-processing service, said that its September data showed improving sales among US small businesses. However, the company reports that consumer behavior remains selective and that traffic has been weaker even as customers spend more when they do shop.

after newsletter promotion

Economic growth continued in the third quarter.

Overall, US manufacturing remained firmly in expansion territory in September. The Institute for Supply Management’s Manufacturing Purchasing Manager’s Index marked its ninth consecutive month of growth after years of contraction. Despite rising prices, new orders, production and employment all remained expansionary and order backlogs increased. As usual, the ISM reported yet another month of expansion in the service sector (it’s been 27 consecutive months) with new orders remaining “particularly strong”.

The Wall Street Journal and other media sources reported recently that first-quarter annualized growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%, and second-quarter growth was increased to 2.2% from 1.5%, which, its editors argued , shows that the “US economy is performing considerably better than pessimistic headlines imply”.

Philadelphia lags in business creation.

My business is based in Philadelphia, a heavily Democratic area in a swing state. My clients appear to mostly be doing well so far this year but, like most small businesses around the country, continue to struggle navigating higher costs and a tight labor market.

This anecdotal evidence is somewhat supported by a May survey by WSFS Bank that found “surprisingly strong confidence among Philadelphia-area businesses” despite inflation and economic uncertainty. In that study, 92% of owners and business decision-makers say their companies are meeting or exceeding expectations, while 66% anticipate growth during the next year.

Philadelphia, however, has its own unique problems, particularly adding fewer small businesses per capita than other large cities. A recent study from Pew Research found that the number of Black-, Hispanic- and female-owned small businesses increased 39% between 2012 and 2022, showing meaningful entrepreneurial growth, but barriers including access to capital, regulatory requirements, taxes, commercial space and the difficulty of scaling companies continued to restrain business formation in the city.

The Democratic strategist James Carville once said that when it comes to electing candidates, “it’s the economy, stupid”. The good news for the Republicans is that the economy is resilient and the overall mood of the country’s small businesses is generally optimistic, despite the many challenges they face. But will that overcome the president’s low approval ratings?

stories.body:
As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner

‘D on’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer , not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.

Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.

Many reacted with revulsion to last year’s unveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood . After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear in feature-length film Misaligned .

Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity.

But AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as the de-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny .

Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases – Hell Grind , a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.”

Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”?

Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive. First, visual “assets” are created of the characters – detailed body-length shots and facial closeups that are used to establish continuity when fed into video-generation prompts. Then, using the assets as an anchor point, each 30-second segment is defined in a 4,000-word prompt (itself partly generated by an LLM) defining the key parameters: action, camera movement, lighting and, of course, the emotions on display. The prompts are revised and the scene regenerated until the uncanny valley is hopefully bridged.

Where, say, Klaus Kinski could summon torrents of rage by tapping into his personal demons, an AI programmer has to achieve the same effect in much more approximate ways. “An AI is not an actor, so how do you communicate the internal state of a character?” says Zack London, who as Gossip Goblin makes highly baroque AI-generated sci-fi shorts. “You can say: they look confused, or they say this in jest, or they say this sternly. But it’s such a broad stroke. The model will probably come out with a very over-the-top telenovela-type performance, or will just not understand.” At that point, it becomes a case of treating the model like a “marionette doll” and tweaking individual strings. “You could say: there’s a slight quiver on the left side of their lip, and then their gaze diverts slightly downwards, and they look up again and blink.”

London chooses to keep a human ghost in the machine by first recording dialogue with real actors, around which he retro-fits the animation. He is candid about the shortcomings of the current prompting process, saying the results suit a certain type of film: “The acting is not going to be particularly subtle, like some grand Anthony Hopkins or Olivia Colman performance. It’s more like an old-school Terry Gilliam or Guy Ritchie performance, where the characters are larger than life.” But maybe that’s where the danger lies for actors: many blockbuster performances, meting out simple beats of easily comprehensible emotion, have a cut-and-paste quality – and are therefore susceptible to AI.

Then again, a mundane magic still happens even on blockbuster sets. “Sometimes the most brilliant moment happens in the fraction of a second. And you can’t put your finger on why an actor gives a certain look,” says Tye Sheridan , the co-founder (in 2016) of Wonder Dynamics, an Autodesk company who developed the AI production tool Autodesk Flow Studio. He should know: he was the star of Steven Spielberg’s 2018 film Ready Player One , which itself patrolled the frontier between real and digital.

Sheridan shares Higgsfield’s belief that AI-driven methods can democratise film-making. But he is adamant that performances should retain a human core. Flow Studio uses AI for an augmented and far cheaper version of motion capture, layering CG characters and environments on top of filmed footage. At Framestore, Webber is exploring similar AI tools that allow him to apply what he calls “digital makeup” to traditional performances, without the guesswork involved in generative prompts.

He, London and Sheridan agree that this hybrid form of film-making still allows actors to make specific choices essential to authentic creation. “You have to ask, with these generative models: are they really designed to deliver legendary performances, or are they designed to cut to an average?” asks Sheridan. Alimzhanov, though, insists something akin to an actor’s internal process is achievable via AI. The prompting used on The Cully Hill Boys was different in one key regard: instead of replicating emotions by specifying the physical mechanics, the AI model generated sequences based on contextual input about what the characters were experiencing.

These two camps of AI acting – technological and human-centric – are fighting the latest bout in the struggle between the forces that have shaped the craft: external v internal; reproducing v experiencing; Laurence Olivier telling Dustin Hoffman that, instead of staying awake for 72 hours, he should “try acting, dear boy”. But where Stanislavsky promoted the internal quest to revitalise acting, this could be the first time in the modern era when the formalist approach – the mannered reproduction of emotions – looks like the future.

Opening the digital floodgates could lead to William Gibson territory , where deathless virtual stars seduce the masses, as in his 1996 novel Idoru. But it’s still not clear whether the box office demand, and thus a true economic case, for AI cinema exists. And we’re yet to see a compelling script that crystallises the possibilities of the tech in story form, as The Matrix did for CGI. If we’re inundated with unloved AI abominations, the words of Val Kilmer in Tombstone, playing that icon of human mortality, Doc Holliday, will ring anew: “There’s just something about him. Something around the eyes reminds me of … me. I’m sure of it – I hate him.”

stories.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wins dismissal of sister's lawsuit
stories.summary: A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 18 minutes ago

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has won a dismissal of a lawsuit brought against him by his sister that claimed he had sexually abused her more than two decades ago.

A US district judge dismissed the case after Ann Altman had refused to attend an independent medical examination, adding she was warned a failure to do so would result in the case being thrown out.

Ann Altman had claimed the OpenAI founder had regularly sexually abused her between 1997 and 2006. Sam Altman has denied those accusations.

The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and they have supported her financially, adding the claims were made as she continued to demand more funds.

District Judge Zachary Bluestone said that despite multiple accommodations and multiple opportunities to do so, Ann Altman did not appear for an independent medical exam on three separate occasions, and "failed to meaningfully prosecute her case".

"Because Annie has continued to violate her discovery obligations and forced this case to a halt through her intransigence, the Court has run out of options and, thus, dismisses her claims with prejudice," he said in his written order.

The case was filed on 6 January 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri.

In it, Ann Altman claimed that her older brother Sam Altman began abusing her when she was three, and he was 12.

However, in a joint statement released by Sam Altman along with his mother and two brothers at the time, the family said they were concerned for Ann Altman's wellbeing and have spent years trying to support her financially and to look after her wellbeing.

The family said she receives monthly financial support, and her bills and rent were also covered, while also trying to assist with medical help.

The statement said her claims against Sam Altman had changed drastically over time, but all of those claims were "utterly untrue".

Sam Altman is the co-founder of OpenAI, which launched its popular ChatGPT artificial intelligence chatbot in 2022.

stories.title: China's growth accelerates as AI boom helps boost exports
stories.summary: Exports have helped offset weak spending at home, but trade tensions and AI doubts cloud its outlook.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026

China's economic growth picked up in the three months to the end of September, rebounding from a three-year low as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom helped boost exports.

The world's second largest economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter, up from the previous period but below the 5% expansion recorded from January to March, according to official Chinese data.

The latest figure is at the bottom end of Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5%-5%, which analysts have said gives policymakers room to address the country's economic challenges.

While exports have helped offset weak spending at home, global trade tensions and uncertainty over AI investments are clouding its outlook.

China's National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that the economy "sustained steady development against pressure" and showed "momentum with new growth drivers and improving structure".

With exports climbing, China's trade surplus - the amount of goods and services it sells abroad compared to what it buys from other countries - is on track to overtake the record $1.2tn (£900bn) seen last year.

Sales of high-tech goods rose by 14.3% while the production of both batteries and industrial robots grew by more than 29%, official figures showed.

Oxford Economics researcher Sheana Yue said manufacturing and high-tech exports have boosted China's growth, despite weak investment and domestic spending.

But property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months from the same period last year, official data also showed.

China's economy has been struggling to shake off a long-running property slump, after years of overbuilding and excessive borrowing by private developers.

There are still no signs that this trend will end soon, Yue said.

Trade uncertainties and geopolitical issues have also made Chinese consumers more "pessimistic" and unwilling to spend, she added.

'Investing in people': Can China's new push to boost spending revive the economy? Published 10 March

Faisal Islam: Why China and AI are worrying global finance bosses Published 3 days ago

The effects of Beijing's targeted support measures for businesses have yet to be seen, said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics.

Several risks stand out from the data, including China's reliance on a "single external engine" in exports, he added.

The technology industry has been a key driver of China's growth in recent quarters.

Global demand for computer chips and other components used to build AI data centres has helped to ease pressure on Beijing and cushion the impact of sluggish domestic consumption.

Chinese businesses have leaned heavily on exports as a prolonged property slump, weak wage growth and high youth unemployment have weighed on consumer spending at home.

In September, Beijing unveiled a raft of support measures, including lower interest rates for some businesses and subsidies for property buyers, in an effort to boost the economy.

But Beijing is facing a backlash from Western economies - including the US and European Union - as manufacturers struggle to compete with large amounts of cheap Chinese goods.

There are also concerns over the billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the companies making those investments can deliver on their promises of generating huge profits.

stories.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
stories.summary: Revolut was one of the hardest hit, with banking services going down for many customers.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Revolut was among UK banking services seemingly affected by the Google Cloud outage on Tuesday

Published 20 October 2026, 09:46 BST

Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard , external , where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

Banking services disrupted

Banks appeared to be among the most badly affected, with customers reporting problems ranging from being unable to access funds abroad to struggling to complete a property purchase.

Rachael Ellen, 25, a Revolut customer from Glasgow, told BBC News she was left unable to access her money.

"Today I was unable to pay for my parking at a shopping centre because my Revolut account wasn't working properly," she told the BBC.

"This left me in a difficult situation as I had no way to access the money I needed at the time."

She said the outage also meant she could not view a transaction from a relative and was told by the app's help bot that there were no pending incoming transactions.

"It's frustrating not knowing where the payment is or when I'll receive it," Rachael added.

Rachael Ellen said the outage caused her "real inconvenience" when she couldn't access her funds on Revolut

More than 1,500 reports of issues affecting Revolut services were flagged to platform outage monitor shortly after 08:00 BST on Tuesday.

A spokesperson for the company said some Revolut services were disrupted earlier as a result of the Google Cloud outage.

"We can confirm that services are now fully restored. Our customers' money and data are safe and remained safe throughout.

"We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

Customers of Lloyds Bank, Halifax and Bank of Scotland - all owned by the Lloyds Banking Group - also reported issues affecting some online banking services.

A Lloyds spokesperson did not confirm the cause of issues affecting some of its services, but told the BBC later on Tuesday "we understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon".

'Incredibly frustrating'

Guy Baybutt, who works for a family-run business The Veg Box Company also said he was "severely affected" by Tuesday's outage.

Baybutt, who is from Preston, told the BBC the firm - which supplies fresh fruit, vegetables and other produce to customers across the UK - could not access its website to download and process customer orders amid the technical issues.

"We were also unable to book parcels onto DPD's system for collection, meaning orders that should have been dispatched today were at risk of being delayed," he said.

"To make matters worse, customers were unable to access our website to place new orders, meaning we lost valuable sales during the outage."

He said that such disruptions can have "serious financial consequences" for small businesses like his own.

"We don't have the resources of larger companies to simply absorb lost revenue, particularly when we're dealing with fresh, perishable produce that needs to reach customers promptly," Baybutt added.

Guy Baybutt told the BBC its services had recovered, but it was frustrating "that a technical failure completely outside our control brought so much of our business to a standstill"

Dependent on the cloud

Tuesday's incident came exactly one year after more than 1,000 sites, including UK banks, were knocked offline for hours during an outage at AWS' largest cloud site .

Experts say this latest outage show how many businesses still rely on core services provided by a few large cloud operators.

"Google Cloud's outage is a reminder of how deeply our economies depend on just a handful of cloud providers," said Prof Feng Li, associate dean for research & innovation at Bayes Business School.

He added that it was not yet clear what caused the power problem identified by Google Cloud.

"Large cloud systems are complex, and failures will happen.

"What matters is how far they spread, how quickly services recover and whether customers have workable alternatives," he added.
